title: MacOS
subtitle: MacOS is reasonably private out of the box but has several high-impact settings that are off or misconfigured by default. Check off each setting as you complete it.

context.title: Before you start
context.body: Most of these settings require your admin password. Go through them in order - FileVault in particular needs a restart to take effect and you'll want to save your recovery key somewhere secure before you begin.

items.name: Enable FileVault full-disk encryption
items.why: FileVault encrypts your entire drive. Without it, anyone with physical access to your Mac - including law enforcement with a warrant - can extract your files by booting from an external drive, bypassing your login password entirely.

steps.text: Open `System Settings` → `Privacy & Security` → scroll to `FileVault` → click `Turn On`
Choose to create a local recovery key - do NOT use your iCloud account as the only recovery option
Save the recovery key in your password manager and somewhere physically secure (not on the computer itself)
Restart your Mac - encryption runs in the background and may take an hour or more on first run

items.name: Enable automatic software updates
items.path: System Settings → General → Software Update → Automatic Updates
items.why: Software updates patch known security vulnerabilities. Attackers actively exploit unpatched systems - running an outdated OS is one of the most common entry points for malware and intrusion.

steps.text: Open `System Settings` → `General` → `Software Update`
Click the info icon next to `Automatic Updates` and enable all options: Check for updates, Download, Install macOS updates, Install app updates, and Install security responses
Restart your Mac daily to ensure updates are applied promptly

items.name: Enable Firewall
items.why: macOS's built-in firewall blocks unsolicited incoming network connections. It's off by default - a strange choice - but takes one click to enable. Particularly important on public Wi-Fi.

steps.text: Go to `System Settings` → `Network` → `Firewall`
Toggle `Firewall` on
Click `Options` and enable `Enable stealth mode` - this prevents your Mac from responding to network probe requests

items.name: Audit app permissions (camera, mic, location)
items.why: macOS apps request access to your camera, microphone, location, contacts, and calendar. Many accumulate permissions over time that they no longer need. Auditing these periodically removes unnecessary access.

steps.text: Open `System Settings` → `Privacy & Security`
Work through each category: `Location Services`, `Microphone`, `Camera`, `Contacts`, `Calendars`
Remove access for any app that doesn't have a clear reason to need it. When in doubt, revoke and see if anything breaks
Under `Location Services` → `System Services`, disable `Location-Based Suggestions` and `Significant Locations`

items.name: Disable Siri & Spotlight data sharing
items.why: Siri sends your queries and Spotlight search terms to Apple servers by default to improve suggestions. This includes things you type into Spotlight - file names, app names, search terms - which can reveal a lot about your activity and habits.

steps.text: Open `System Settings` → `Siri & Spotlight`
Toggle off `Ask Siri` if you don't use it
Under `Siri Suggestions`, disable `Suggestions in Search`, `Suggestions in Look Up`, and `Suggestions on Lock Screen`
Open `System Settings` → `Privacy & Security` → `Analytics & Improvements` and uncheck `Improve Siri & Dictation` and `Share Mac Analytics`

items.name: Disable advertising identifier & personalized ads
items.path: System Settings → Privacy & Security → Apple Advertising
items.why: Apple assigns your Mac an advertising identifier used to target ads across Apple's platforms. Disabling personalized ads limits how Apple and third-party developers can use your activity data for ad targeting.

steps.text: Open `System Settings` → `Privacy & Security` → `Apple Advertising`
Toggle off `Personalized Ads`

items.name: Lock screen - require password immediately
items.why: A Mac that doesn't require a password after sleep is physically unprotected. Anyone who walks up to your laptop when the screen wakes has full access to everything on it.

steps.text: Open `System Settings` → `Lock Screen`
Set `Require password after screen saver begins or display is turned off` to `Immediately`
Set `Start screen saver when inactive` to 5 minutes or less

items.name: Install antivirus / threat protection
items.why: macOS has built-in malware protection (XProtect, Gatekeeper) that handles the most common threats. For most users this is sufficient. If you download files from unofficial sources, an antivirus adds an extra layer.

steps.text: `Malwarebytes` - free version scans on demand, paid version adds real-time protection
`Bitdefender` - strong detection rates, lightweight performance impact
`NordVPN Threat Protection Pro` - blocks malicious URLs and ads in addition to malware scanning

items.name: Disable sharing services you don't use
items.why: macOS enables several network sharing services that expose your Mac to local network discovery. Unless you actively use them, they represent unnecessary attack surface - especially on public or shared networks.

steps.text: Go to `System Settings` → `General` → `Sharing`
Turn off everything you don't actively use: `File Sharing`, `Screen Sharing`, `Remote Login`, `Remote Management`, `Bluetooth Sharing`
Check your computer name at the top - avoid using your real name in it

items.name: Optional - Standard user account
items.why: By default, the user account created when setting up a Mac is an Administrator account. Mac's have many mechanisms in place to defend against abusive admin actions but vulnerabilities have cropped up in the past. If you would like an extra layer of security, you can create and use a Standard user account instead. Whenever you must take an admin action, you will be prompted to enter your admin credentials. This guide assumes you already have your Mac set up and need to change your Administrator user to a Standard user. It's essential that you verify you have a second functioning Administrator account that you can log into before demoting your primary user account.

steps.text: Go to `System Settings` → `Users & Groups`
Verify you have a separate Administrator account that you can log into
If a second Administrator account doesn't exist, create one
Log out of your user profile that you plan to demote
Log in as the backup Administrator
Go to `System Settings` → `Users & Groups`
Click on the `i` icon next to the user account you wish to demote
Toggle off `Allow this user to administer this computer`
Enter the username and password for the Administrator account you're currently logged into if prompted

If you have FileVault enabled, verify your demoted account can still log in after a reboot - `System Settings` → `Privacy & Security` → `FileVault` → check for an `Enable Users` button. If one doesn't exist, disregard
Reboot your computer to apply changes
Log back in as your newly demoted user account
